paragraphs.text: Lesson one, double trouble.
Mary and Jacob are a married couple with two children who are rather mischievous.
Listen to their conversation as you try to answer the comprehension questions.
I'm completely wiped out from chasing the kids around all day.
Let me tell you honey, back when we talked about having kids I didn't know it was going to be so exhausting.
I just can't get over how much damage a pair of four-year-old twins can do to one house.
Yesterday they had a chocolate pudding fight in the kitchen.
It took me over three hours to clean putting off the kitchen walls.
If you think that's bad, you ought to see what they did to my new tackle box.
They took out all of my new hooks and filled the box with mud.
And when I asked them why, they told me they wanted mud for a mud pie the next time we went fishing.
I can top that.
Last week I found Alex and Matthew in the upstairs bathroom looking into the toilet.
I knew they had done something.
Oh no, they didn't. Please tell me they didn't.
They flushed the baby turtle we got them down the toilet.
They told me they wanted to see how long the baby turtle could hold its breath.
I was wondering where that turtle wandered off to.
I should have known better than to bottom a pet.
When I saw it missing, well, I just couldn't bring myself to ask what happened to it.
It was hard enough taking care of two babies, but when they were infants at least they stayed put.
I think it's even harder now that they're running around and wreaking havoc.
Just wait until they hit the teenage years.
Let's not even think about that right now.
Will you just look at this living room?
It's going to take us a decade just to clean up in here.
How in the world did Alex and Matthew get into the watercolor paints?
I thought you hid them.
I did. I promise. I hid the paints where Alex and Matthew would never find them.
They were in your sock drawer, weren't they?
I...yeah, they were. I guess no place is safe.
Speaking of which, how did they get the cookies down from the top of the refrigerator?
Alex helps Matthew climb up onto the kitchen counter and then Matthew grabs the cookies.
At least they're learning teamwork.
Ha ha. True. I have to confess. My siblings and I caused a ton of trouble when we were kids.
I guess they're taking after their dad.
And you were still a bit of a rebel when I met you.
I cleaned up my act before we got married though.
Well, let's hope the boys follow in your footsteps and turn into responsible adults. Some day.
Come on. We might as well start cleaning the paint off the walls while the little guys are taking their nap.
And when they wake up, I'm going to put them to work right alongside us.
At least that way they can't get into any more mischief.
Now let's learn the vocabulary from the conversation.
Mary says, I'm completely wiped out from chasing the kids around all day.
The phrasal verb, wiped out, means extremely tired. No more energy.
At the end of a long hard day, you can say, I'm completely wiped out.
Then she says, let me tell you honey.
The word honey in this case is an affectionate nickname that people who are married or in romantic relationships use for each other.
Jacob says, I just can't get over how much damage a pair of four-year-old twins can do to one house.
If you say you can't get over something, it means you can't comprehend or can't accept it because it's so surprising or shocking.
Jacob and Mary's children are twins. Twins are two brothers or sisters who are born together at the same time.
Mary says that yesterday the boys had a chocolate pudding fight in the kitchen.
Chocolate pudding is a type of dessert. Pudding is like a thick, sweet liquid.
Jacob tells Mary about something that the kids did to his new tackle box.
A tackle box is a box that holds fishing equipment.
One piece of fishing equipment is hooks. Hooks are curved pieces of metal.
Mary responds, I can top that.
This expression, I can top that means I have a better story than that one.
You can say, I can top that when you are about to tell a story that's even bigger or more impressive than what the other person just said.
Mary describes how the kids flushed the baby turtle down the toilet.
The verb flushed means they made the water go down the toilet.
Jacob says, I was wondering where that turtle wandered off to.
Wondered off means went without direction. The verb wander means to go without a particular destination.
Jacob says that when he saw the turtle missing, he just couldn't bring himself to ask what happened to it.
This phrase, I couldn't bring myself to ask, means I couldn't manage to ask.
If you couldn't bring yourself to do something, it means you want to or you try to do something, but you just can't force yourself to do so.
Mary points out that when the kids were infants, at least they stayed put.
This expression, stay put, means to stay in one place.
But now the boys are running around and wreaking havoc.
Wreaking havoc means causing trouble or destruction.
After the mess that the boys made in the living room, Mary says it's going to take us a decade just to clean up in here.
A decade is a period of ten years.
She asks, how in the world did Alex and Matthew get into the watercolor paints?
In this question, how in the world, adding in the world expresses surprise or shock.
There are several other ways to do this.
You can ask, how on earth?
Or, how the heck?
Or even, how the hell?
How the hell is the strongest and can be offensive?
People often add the hell to questions when they are angry.
Jacob says he hid the paints where Alex and Matthew would never find them, but Mary says, they were in your sock drawer, weren't they?
This phrase, weren't they, is a question tag.
It makes a statement into a question which you expect the answer to be yes, and you're just asking to confirm it.
And Mary was right, the paints were hidden in Jacob's sock drawer.
Jacob asks how the kids can get the cookies down from the top of the refrigerator, and Mary says they use teamwork.
Teamwork is the ability to cooperate and work together, helping each other to reach a goal.
Jacob says that he and his siblings also caused a ton of trouble when they were kids.
The word siblings refers to brothers and sisters without specifying the gender.
A ton of trouble means a lot of trouble.
Jacob then says that his kids are taking after their dad.
The phrasal verb taking after means acting similar to an older family member.
Mary says that Jacob was still a bit of a rebel when she met him.
The word rebel in this context refers to someone who likes to break rules and challenge authority.
But Jacob says, I cleaned up my act before we got married though.
This phrase, I cleaned up my act means I started behaving responsibly.
I stopped doing bad things.
Mary says, let's hope the boys follow in your footsteps.
To follow in someone's footsteps means to do the same actions or take the same life path as that person.
Finally, Jacob suggests starting to clean up while the boys are taking their nap.
A nap is a short period of sleep in the middle of the day.
Children often take naps, but adults can also take naps.
And Mary says that she's going to make the boys help them clean up.
At least that way they can't get into any more mischief.
Mischief is behavior that causes annoyance or trouble.
And mischief usually has a playful connotation, not serious bad trouble.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
